utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I'd like to go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes. Since some protective measures apply to the next witness, Madam Usher, you are invited to pull the curtains down. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Before the next witness, Witness 61, comes to testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- I do request that with regard to the manner of examination, that the Prosecution - and I've spoken to Mr. Re about this - be exceedingly careful with the use of leading questions. I do not intend on interrupting the testimony of this witness at all by -- avoided by the interventions but would request by virtue of the kind of testimony and the nature of testimony that we're about to see and considering that the Rules, as they exist, be particularly careful in this regard with the use of leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how the rules on leading questions are. The case law is perhaps not as settled as it may be in many domestic jurisdictions, but, Mr. Re, you've understood the wish of Mr. Guy-Smith that leading should be avoided to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's particularly why I believe it's Rule 96, as it relates of our rules, Rule 96, which deals with the issues concerning corroboration or the lack of necessity thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, you had not the rules on leading questions but the rules of evidence in general terms under Rule 96?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please the assist in coming a bit closer to the ... Witness, I will call you Witness 61 because we will not use your name in this courtroom; that is part of the protective measures that have been granted in respect of you. Witness 61, before you give evidence, the rules of this court require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Since I understand that you can't read - is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore I will give you the text of that solemn declaration and I'd like you to -- I'd invite you to repeat my words. I solemnly declare -- could you please repeat these words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that I will speak the truth --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I will speak the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the whole truth, nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This solemn declaration means that whatever answer you give should be not only in accordance with the truth, but also everything -- you don't have to repeat my words anymore. I'm just explaining to you what it means; that is, that all your answers have to be fully truthful. We will not use your name, and if there are any questions which might identify you or your answers might identify you, then the party that is examining you will ask to go into private session. The outside world cannot see your face. They can hear what you say but they can't see your face. Mr. Re, are you ready to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We'll have to move into private session for the beginning of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we go back into private session for one moment. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Witness 61, a moment ago I was asking you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise. If we could go back into private session for a moment. I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- I do apologise. Something just dawned on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber would appreciate if not more than five times in two minutes we have to change from private session to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 61, a moment ago I was asking you about your seeing the KLA when you went to visit your brother-in-law in the village. How did you know they were KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had KLA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you recognise them as KLA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you ask me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you know that they were KLA uniforms, as distinct to, say, Serbian uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the Serbian uniforms, but I know how KLA uniforms were. I remember them. I know how they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were these KLA soldiers doing when you saw them in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went around to the place. They did nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, perhaps as far as the uniforms are concerned we could invite the witness to describe them. Could you tell us -- you said you know how KLA uniforms were. Could you describe them to me. What colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in a colour of -- I didn't -- I don't know exactly because I was not very much interested in colours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What else could you then tell us about these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had something on the sleeves. I don't know how you call them. I don't know how you can describe them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What size approximately was it? That there was on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not big. It had them exactly here. It was not big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said "exactly here," you were pointing at the upper arm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the right or on the left side. I was not interested to know exactly. Of course I was looking after my own business, so I took no interest to see where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what you saw, could you indicate what size it approximately was, perhaps with your fingers like this, like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness with her hands makes a gesture of something, let's say, 10 to 15 centimetres, something there of a guide. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P9 while that's coming up on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first ask the witness about whether she remembers the colour of what was on the sleeves. Do you remember what you said was on the upper arms? What colour was it, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in black letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from the letters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yellow in black letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just yellow or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think black, yellow then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the label said, what letters they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe "UCK," I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the uniforms have any patterns on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were in camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness had please be shown Exhibit P9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise and I hope I'm not being unduly pedantic, but the witness has given evidence in respect of her recollection of the colour and lettering on the patches, which does not accord with what Mr. Re is about to show her as far as I understand it. And if one is asking about leading questions to put to a witness, a symbol which has not been put to her before and which is inconsistent with evidence that she's given in chief in order to seek a recognition of it, it is not in our submission the appropriate way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson [sic], was it put to the witness before? Was what we see on P9, which is not yet on our screen and should not be on this screen at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? Well, then we have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have been clearer in instructing the registrar that where there was an objection -- of course, not every time when something is put on the screen my explicit permission is required, but I should have been more cautious here that it should not be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'd rather taken Your Honour's indication to Mr. Re that a foundation ought to be laid before the image was put to be a pretty clear indication that the way the matter's been dealt with is the way it shouldn't have been -- been dealt with. But I'm not -- I'm going to withdraw my objection because the -- as we say in England, the horse has bolted and there's no point trying to close the stable door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the image on the screen in front of you, Witness 61. Do you recognise that image?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please look at the screen again, I see you're not looking at the screen, and could you tell us whether this is or is not what you saw on the upper arms of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's UCK, it's -- that's UCK. I didn't see them exactly. This is in red and black and then the letters were -- are here in yellow. I didn't see them exactly because I didn't have much time, I didn't go out of my house frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the time when you saw KLA soldiers in the village, were there still Serbian police in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were there, but then they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know when they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the time. I only know that they withdrew from the village. I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you say about how long before you and your family left the village the Serbian police withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They withdrew before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know why they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know really. I only saw them withdrawing. I don't know the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a little earlier, Witness 61, that your husband told you about KLA soldiers in the village. What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he went out to work he saw them, and he knew the Togeri. I didn't know him. He described me, he talked to me about the Toger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about this Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came home, he took us, and then he told me that this is the Toger, because I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about one night when you were at home in your village. I'm going to ask you some questions and I want you to slowly tell the Trial Chamber about what happened that night. And the first thing I'm going to ask you is: Can you try and remember when this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the date when it happened. It was at 12.00 at night. Toger came with four other people. He came to the door. My father-in-law came up and opened the door for them. He opened the door. They came inside. My father-in-law asked them, What do you want? They asked him, Where is your son? My father-in-law told them that he is sleeping. Then they took us. They waited for us until we dressed. Then they came inside the house again. They told the father -- my father-in-law that, You should not expect that they will send us back. So they take us then to the staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- they put my husband --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just ask you to pause there and I'll come to that in a moment. I just want to make sure we get some of the details of the story clear for the Judges. Okay? Now, I just want to go back to when it happened. You said you don't know the date. What time of year was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I really don't know. It should have been 1998/1997, I don't remember dates. Most probably it was 1998 or maybe 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What time of year was it? You've got four seasons, summer, winter, autumn, and spring.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, how can I say? It was spring-time. It was not cold. It was hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What year did you leave the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long before you left the village did this happen? Or how long after this happened did you leave the village, to put it the other way around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was two weeks after this happened, I think so, after two weeks we left the village. Maybe three weeks, I'm not really sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. You said -- I'll just stop you there for a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I ask one additional question. You earlier told us that the Serbian police withdrew from the village. Now, this event you're describing, was that after or before the Serbian police had withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this happened after they withdrew, after the police forces had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was it the same year that the Serbian police forces withdrew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember the exact date when they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I do apologise for rising. I've been informed that there may be some difficulty with translation with regard to page 17, line 13, in terms of whether or not the statement made was whether or not to expect anybody back or not, which I think is of some importance. I'm wondering whether or not we can get that cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's a translation problem, I think, Mr. Re, could you please then clarify that. Perhaps again ask the witness what they told the father-in-law at that occasion. Witness, could you - because there might be a translation problem - could you again tell us what those who came at your door-step at night, what they told your father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told the father-in-law -- well, now I'm not able to recall quite well, but they said -- my father-in-law asked, What do you want my son for? And they said, We have to ask him about something. And the old man said, If you need him for something, here I am for you. You are Albanians, I am Albanian. And they didn't care what he said. He went inside the house. We were inside. We were in bed. We got up. Then they went out. We dressed up and we went out as well. Well, I'm not recalling things properly anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now in your earlier answer there was something in it about sent back, that's at least how it was translated to us. It reads: "You should not expect that they will send us back." Could you tell us exactly what you meant with the words you then spoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I told him -- now that they took us away, do not expect us to be alive and come back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you told your father-in-law. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is not what I said to my father-in-law, but I was just thinking in that way, that I was not expecting myself to go back alive home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why weren't you expecting yourself to get back alive home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is what I heard, I had heard. This is what I thought. I've never seen what has happened, but I just had heard about things, about the others, and I thought, Well, me as well, I'll not be able to come back home. Well, it was only God saving us and we could come back home with our children, to our children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What things had you heard about others that made you think that you may not come back home?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm rising to interpose an objection at this time, of hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the objection is denied, but you are invited to explore as good as you can the sources of the hearsay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about what you had heard, and I want you to tell the Judges who told you whatever you'd heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband, he had heard from others and he came home, told us about what he had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he say he had heard and whom did he say he had heard it from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If -- well, I make the same -- make the same submission, and I think perhaps it would be appropriate to reverse the order of the questions as to make a determination of who was the source first before we get into what was said because it may -- it may be of -- of help to the Chamber to make a determination of how many sources out -- were coming, and whether or not this is in fact attributed to any particular individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sequence of questions, we'll leave that to Mr. Re at this moment, at least if he explores as good as he can the issues; that is, who was the source, if it's, of course, a second- or third-hand hearsay then of course the Chamber would be very cautious in interpreting it. But, Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were telling the Court that your husband had told you things. I want you to tell the Court what he had told you and who he said had told him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who had told him, but what I know is that he had told us about people being killed, that he had done massacres, this is what he had heard while he was moving around in the village and this is what he told us at home. That's why we were scared of him and that is why we were thinking that we wouldn't be able to come back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "he had done massacres," who did your husband had -- was the "he" who had done massacres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was about Toger.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did your husband tell you about people being killed or what he'd heard about people being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say exactly. I don't know really how they had killed people. This is all what he had heard about these people being killed, that's all. In fact, I was not interested to know more about things. He was just caring about his business and I was caring about things at home. We were many people living in the same house, and we were very scared all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you scared of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were scared of him. Before -- before we were taken away by him, we were not afraid; but after that moment, we kept being scared all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was -- what was Toger and the four men he was with wearing? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you describe the weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well -- well, I've seen them when they came in the house. They had knives, they had pistols, they had a knife, a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before when you were talking about KLA soldiers you told the Judges that they had something on their sleeves. Did these five men have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had the insignia of the KLA, the UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did they have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had them on the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you remember which part of the arm, upper arm, lower arm, middle arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the upper arm, on the right or left, I can't remember quite well, because it was dark and I couldn't see them quite well and I was very scared all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did they treat you, these five men when they came to the house? How did they behave towards you and your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't say anything. My husband -- they took away my husband. Two people with him and two other people were with me and they took us to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did they do to your husband? You said they took him away. What did they do to take him away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they tied him with his hands behind and they tied him to the well. They also took me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we just move into private session for one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago, Witness 61, you said that the -- these five men, Toger and the four others, took you to KLA headquarters. Where -- describe what the KLA -- describe what this location was. Was it a building? Was it a farm? Was it a house? That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was a house. There were Albanians living there. It was a one-floor house. A woman used to live there, but she had left her house and she was not living there any longer. She had left the country and she was living abroad, and this is where they took us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said they'd tied your husband's hands behind his back. What did they do with your husband when you got to this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They sent him to the well, and when I was inside they asked -- they asked me some questions, Toger asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whereabouts inside the house was this that Toger asked you the questions? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the room, inside the room. It was the room where he was staying. He invited me to sit down. He was asking whether my husband was -- had been working with the police forces, collaborating with the police forces; and I said no. We -- I told him we've been always on good terms with Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. When you went into that room, was there anybody else in the room when you went in, apart from you and Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only me and Toger. There was another person staying at the door, and then he said, this person, You may leave. If I need you, I will call you back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did Toger spend asking you questions, such as whether your husband had been working with the police forces or collaborating with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember well. It should have been around half an hour asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said he invited you to sit down. Tell the Trial Chamber what furniture was in that room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a table in front of him, chairs, a TV set, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why do you think he was staying in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a bed as well. I don't know why he was there. This is the room he was staying. This is all I know. I don't know more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When he was asking you these questions, where was he and where were you in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was on the chair on one side, and I was sitting on another chair on the other side. He was keeping down notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he do with these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. He simply wrote down something. I don't know what he wrote. He asked me about whether we had links with the police or not, and maybe he wrote about these things. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he show you the notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he ask you to sign anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Toger have any weapons when he was questioning you in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had but he removed them and he put them on the table. He had the knife, he had a pistol, and then he took them and put them on the table. Then there was a guard, and he told him to bring him a wooden stick. And then he took the wooden stick and he put it on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did the guard do after Toger asked him to put the wooden stick on the table -- after he put the wooden stick on the table, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards brought it and went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you wearing that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me, I was wearing a short dress, also a blouse and a pair of sandals, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the lights on or off in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the lights were on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they go off at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he began to -- to do - how can I put it? - it's very hard for me to talk about it. When he began to take me -- when he took me to the bed, he took the light off. Then he undressed me. He told me to go to the bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How were you feeling when he did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood that that was the purpose of him taking us. I thought that was exactly what he took us for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you think that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that I should undress, so I realised that that was the purpose of him taking us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was he wearing when he took you to the bed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Black dresses. He took them off. He undressed, and he began then what he wanted to do, to have fun on me. He did have fun as much as he wanted. I did not dare to scream. I did not dare to say that this was happening. I was so scared, I could not shout, I could not scream; I simply trembled. He asked me why I was shivering. I said -- I told him that I was cold. Then he began what he wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Witness 61, I understand it's very difficult for you to tell the Trial Chamber what he did to you, but I'm going to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber with as much detail as you can remember what he did to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First he began to kiss me on the neck. Then he touched my breasts, and then he did what he wanted several times. Then he had all the fun he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, you said you were undressed and -- were you on the bed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me, Get up and go to the bed, and I went to the bed. And then he came and he did what he wanted to do. The same thing happened like it happens with your husband -- with my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were on the bed, were you lying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first try to find out to what extent is the Defence willing to accept that not every single detail will be repeated here as we find it in the statement. Of course, if there will be cross-examination on details, then of course Mr. Re should elicit the details. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe there's a necessity to go through every single detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could -- would it be acceptable for you if Mr. Re would just briefly summarize what he finds in the statement, put that to the witness, and ask her whether that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm -- Witness 61, I'm going to read something from the statement you made to the Prosecutor last year about what you said happened, and I just want you to listen and tell me if it's correct and, if there's anything that needs correction, you can do so. Okay. What you said was -- this is when you were on the bed at paragraph 7: "He asked me why I was shivering. I said because I was cold. He started to kiss my neck. He placed his hands on my breasts" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "He started to kiss my neck. He placed his hands on my breast and my waist. He forcibly parted my legs and put his penis in my vagina. I had my eyes closed. I was scared and thought I was going to die."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "He ejaculated in my vagina. He then waited a while and raped me again."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "I remember that he placed his penis in my vagina at least one more time until he ejaculated again."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "He also made me lie on my stomach. He placed his penis in my anus and kept it there until he ejaculated."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "In between the times that he raped me, he stayed on the bed alongside of me. I remained on the bed, very much afraid that he would kill me."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Finally, after about one and a half hours he told me that I could get up off from the bed. He told me not to tell my husband what happened."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "I remember that I used my clothes to wipe the sperm from the rapes off of my thighs and legs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "I then got dressed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what happened after you got dressed? How did you leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterward, he told me to go out. I dressed and I went out. They took my husband and brought him in. Then he told me not to tell him anything. I didn't tell him anything until we went home. Then I told -- at home I told my husband, my father-in-law, and everybody else. So we went home. When we went home, I told what had happened to my father-in-law, to my mother-in-law, to every people in the family. I described them what had happened to me. It was something very bad that had happened to me. Then the next morning at 5.00 in the morning, my father-in-law went to the headquarters. He told them what had happened to me and to his son. Then they came and asked me about what had happened. I told them what had happened, what he did to me. Then they asked him. At first he did not admit. He said that I had lied, but it was not true. I told them what had really happened. Then they came to me. They said to me that it was not a lie -- I told them it was not a lie, and that was the truth. Then they went back to him again and they asked him. Then he admitted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back on what you've just said. You said: "Then they came and asked me what had happened." Who was it who came? Did they come to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three people, commanders. They were from our village and from another village, so they came to me and they asked me. And then they went to him and they questioned him. He at first did not admit, but then later he confessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the three people who came, were they from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commanders of UCK, that's how they referred to them; commanders, that's how they were referred. I didn't recognise them, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, for purposes -- for purposes of the record, I object to the hearsay with regard to the issue of any admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was going to explore that, and I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back to these commanders of the UCK, did they refer to themselves as commanders of the UCK or did someone else refer to them as commanders of the UCK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how they were called, "commanders." They were the highest people. I didn't know them. This is what the people my father-in-law talked to and then they came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they wearing when they came to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normal wearing. There was one with UCK uniform; the others were wearing normal dresses, normal clothes like ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. No, they had no weapons -- I think they had no weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said: "They went to him and they questioned him. He at first did not admit it but then later he confessed." Tell the Trial Chamber, the Judges, what -- how you know that and what was told to you about how he admitted and confessed to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came to me and asked me, and then they told me that he had admitted. They told me not to be afraid, he will not do anything to me, that he will not come to us. He will see you in the street and he will not dare talk to you. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they say that to you -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that. How many times did you see these people you referred to as KLA commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only on that day, the day when they came to see me, to question me. I didn't know them. Two people were from our village. The other one, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did they tell you who he had confessed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had confessed to them. They had talked to him. When they came to ask me, they told me that he had said that I had lied. I told them that it was not a lie, it was the truth. I had nothing to lie about because what had happened was really the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see Toger again after that night in that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. One time maybe. I didn't speak to him. He did not harass us, but we were scared. We did not dare to go out. Then we decided to leave the village altogether, so we left the village at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That -- maybe one time that you saw him, where was that? Or describe how you saw him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in his car. He was passing with his car, but he did not speak to us. But we were very scared of him. He passed sometimes next to our road, but he did not speak to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you describe the car? Can you remember what sort of car he had when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A black car, yes a black car, a jeep, a big jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did your family leave the village? I think your evidence earlier was it was about -- two weeks, about, after this happened to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left the village, because that's what everybody did. There was a lot of fighting, so we left the village, like everybody else was doing, and we never returned home. My husband returned once to the house, the house was destroyed, then he came back us to and he joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you returned to your village since then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I have never returned to the village. Only my father-in-law returns sometimes because his two sons are still in Kosova, so he sometimes went back to visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 61, I want you to tell the Trial Chamber, tell the Judges, what Toger looked like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe him, even if I saw him today, now, I cannot -- will not be able to recognise him. I don't know. I know that he was short, not big man, black hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he taller than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a little taller than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What -- how old was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 20, 22, 23, no older than that. I don't know exactly, but he was something around that age. He was young.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What language was he speaking to you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What, please? Albanian. I heard him speaking in Albanian. I don't know what other language he spoke, but that night he spoke to me in Albanian. He was not from our village; he was from another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you remember about his accent? Are you able to say what sort of accent he had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "Albanian," are you meaning from the country of Albania or a part of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the place where he lived. He was not from our village, he was not from our place, he was from another place. I don't know where he came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- you said Toger and four others came to your house that night. How did the other four refer to this person you've called Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They referred to him as Toger. I don't know his name. I remember them calling him, "the Toger."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that how you know him, that he was called Toger, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I'm looking at the clock. I didn't interrupt until now because looking at the statement it might be that you are close to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm almost there. I've just -- there's a photograph I wish to show her in private session. If it's appropriate to take the break now, because it might take a few moments to show her the photograph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are back on the old video system, that means that for redactions we need at least half an hour. Therefore, we'll have a break until five minutes past 11.00. We'll have a break and we'd like to see you back after the break, Witness 61.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 61, before the break I was asking you to describe Toger to the Court, and you said that he was a short man, taller than you. Do you know how tall you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly how tall I am. I've forgotten how tall I've been -- I used to be. It should be a metre something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you saw him that night, what did you notice about his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I remember he had some bumps on the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of bumps and where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on the cheeks and on the lower part of the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just touch your face to show the Judges where you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on the cheeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness was pointing, I would say, the lower parts of the cheeks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about his neck and throat, did you notice anything about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And on the beard -- on the chin, on the chin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think we overlapped there. I was going to ask you about his neck and throat. Did you notice anything about his neck or throat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen anything on the throat. Maybe on the chin he had some pimples, on the cheeks as well, but I was not so much interested to see him on the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just tell me about the -- I think you called them a moment ago "bumps on his face" and then you said "pimples." Can you just describe in a little bit more detail, if you can, what you saw or what sort of bumps or pimples they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were small, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What looked -- what did it look like had caused them, these bumps or pimples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I simply know he had some bumps on the face, but I don't know why and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, before the break you told the Court that Toger and these four men took you and your husband to the KLA headquarters. How did you know or why did you say it was KLA headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is how people called the place. It was the headquarters of the KLA. Everybody was referring to it as such. I've never been -- I was not there with them. This is all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When -- I withdraw that. You've told the Court about Toger and four men coming to your house that night. Did your husband know or recognise Toger when he came to the house that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did your husband know his name when Toger came to the house that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't know his name. We only know that he was called Toger, but we didn't know his name. He didn't know his name and I didn't know his name either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did your husband know him as Toger and recognise him as Toger when he came to the house that night?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have two submissions: One, that it's leading,, and second is that it calls for hearsay, which at this time we have no information about. How he obtained this information, we don't have. More importantly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if the question is -- is put in a slightly different way, not, "Did your husband know," but, "Did your husband tell you whether he --"

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would satisfy part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. The other matter, whether it's leading or not, I think - I think - it's a necessary clarification in view of one of the earlier answers of the witness. So, Mr. Re, you may proceed, and perhaps reformulate the question as far as what the husband knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did your husband know of the person called Toger at the time when Toger came to your house that night?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're using exactly now the same phrasing, Mr. Re, where you were invited to do it differently. Let me. The evening when Toger and the four men came to your house, did your husband at that time say anything to you as far as who it was that came to the house? Did he say, Look there is or there is X, Y, or Z. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we didn't know them at all. We didn't recognise them. They only recognised Toger, and he simply knew that they called him Toger, because he had seen him before and he recognised him when he came inside the house. But I couldn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you did not know Toger, how do you know that your husband recognised the person that came into the house as being Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he had seen him before, he had seen him in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but did he tell you that or did -- or did he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he told me that he is Toger, after we came back home, Toger was the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you learned from your husband after you had returned to your house that your husband when Toger and the four men came in, that he recognised Toger as the man he knew under that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, the Toger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Earlier today you told the Judges that they sent your husband to the well. What did your husband tell you about what happened to him when you were in the room with Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came home, he told me that he had put him in the water to the -- up to the waist line and he had put the lid on the well and that he was left there inside until they finished with me. When I was taken out, they have taken him out, too. He was in water up -- and the water came up to the waist line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see your husband in the well yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. He told me that they put him in the well, and I saw them when they was taking him to the well because the well was near the house. I was sent inside the house, and they -- he was taken to the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who did you see taking him to the well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was two persons only. There were two persons with me taking me to the house and there were two persons with my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said your husband said he had put your husband in the water. Who did he say had put him in the water, in the well, up to his waist line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the other persons who were with Toger, I don't know who they were, I didn't know them. He just told that they had taken him to the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Earlier today you told the Judges about your family leaving the village and you said there was some fighting. Who was the fighting between when you left your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was among themselves, fighting with one another. Well, it was UCK forces with the Serb forces, they were fighting with one another and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we perhaps first try to get a more factual basis for one of the issues. You said your husband told you that he had been put in the well up to his waist. Was there anything you noticed that either confirmed to you what he said or actually did not confirm what he said? Did you observe anything special?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we went home -- well, nothing. He simply said he was taken, he was put in the well. He's never -- he didn't tell me anything what they were asking about. He simply told me that he was put in the well and they'd been -- they were guarding him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you see anything when going home with your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me put it in another way. If someone is put in a well up to his waist in the water, you would expect his clothes to be really wet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, his clothes were wet. Yes, they were wet from the waist downward they were wet, and he changed his clothes when we went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you went home or after you arrived at home did he change his clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we went home, after we were allowed to go back home, I changed his clothes and we stayed at home. And then we went to the headquarters. He and my father-in-law went to the KLA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that immediately after you had come home and after your husband had changed his clothes? Was that that same night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was around 3.00 in the, morning when we went -- 3.00 -- it was at 3.00 in the afternoon that we went home, and at 5.00 in the morning they went to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just try to clarify that. You said you were taken from your home at night, at midnight. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You described the -- you described the events as follows: That you were taken to what you call the headquarters, that for some time questions were put to you, that you were then abused, which took approximately one hour and a half, which all together makes it approximately two and a half to three hours which that would take. And then to go home again, that -- it surprises me if you would have arrived home at 3.00 in the afternoon, because on the basis of what you told us I would rather expect you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was 3.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then there must have been either a translation mistake or you have misspoken. And was it then after a couple of hours that your father-in-law went to see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it all happened that same one night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Had you heard of an organisation called the Black Eagles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Had you heard of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were something black but I haven't seen them, but I didn't went out too often from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you knew they were something black. Just tell the Trial Chamber what knew or what you'd heard about the Black Eagles and who you'd heard it from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you can ask that question when the witness said she wouldn't know the expression "Black Eagles."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, the witness said something -- she denied knowledge of Black Eagles. She said she knew about something black and then you introduced the next question by saying: You told us about something black. What do you know about the Black Eagles? That's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Q. Had you heard of an organisation called the Black Eagles? "A. I don't know. I know that they were something black but I haven't seen them"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question is: Have you -- what did you hear? I -- to me there was some ambiguity there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please rephrase the question in such a way that there could be no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that you had not seen an organisation called the Black Eagles, but you knew they were something black. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband had seen them and he described me the way they were dressed. How can I put it? In -- they had also the insignia on the sleeves. I don't know anything more. I could not come out to see them. I was not interested. I was minding my business. I prepared the food for my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said -- you said your husband had seen them and described the way they were dressed. What did he tell you about the Black Eagles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, again this the -- this is not a way to put this to the witness. You said that your husband described --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had seen them. He went out, he worked, so he had seen them. I haven't seen them. So when he came home --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he told me the way they were dressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that they had this thing on the sleeve --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Is it correctly understood where you referred to something black, that he described them - we'll come to who "them" exactly are - that he described persons dressed in black with insignia? Is that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had UCK dresses and they had the insignia on the arm. I don't know what kind of insignia they wore, but there was some insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did your husband ever give you a clue on how they, that is, the men dressed in black with the insignia, how they were called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't mention any name, but he saw the Toger and his men and he told me they were wearing in black clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you heard a description of the people wearing the clothes, but they were never named as far as you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, only the black clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were wearing such clothes, the black ones. I don't know how they were called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you never heard the name of "Black Hawks" or "Black Eagles" or "black --" is that something your husband never mentioned to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to put it because I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember speaking to an investigator from the Prosecution in August 2002 with a -- a Finnish man called Matti Raatikainen with an Albanian-speaking person called Ardiana?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember giving him a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember giving a statement, but I have forgotten what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your memory of what happened to you and when it happened better in 2002, that is, five years ago when you -- five years ago when you gave the statement than it is now, as to the date when these things happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I say? I don't know what to say. I never forget what had happened to me. I could forget something but not really what happened to me, that's unforgettable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Unless there's any --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If the issue is as to -- might the witness just remove her earphones a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you to take your earphones off for a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If the issue is as to date and date alone, Your Honours should be aware that there are two passages in the statement that Mr. Re is referring to. The first is in the second sentence of the third paragraph in which the witness says: "Since I did not go to school, I don't know what, for example, the months are or mean; therefore, I can't describe the time more precisely." And then two paragraphs further on in the second sentence: "The first problems we had happened somewhere at the end of July or the beginning of August in 1998." Now, if those two statements together are sought to be elicited from the witness so that Your Honours can draw the appropriate inference as to whether the second is reliable in view of the first, then I, for my part, would have no objection to there being a stipulation or an acknowledgement that those two sentences are in the witness statement. Beyond that, there's no basis for memory refreshing, and, with respect, I'm not sure how taken together those two statements can refresh anybody's memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I take it that you -- you would like to draw the attention of the witness to -- to what exactly? So that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the sole basis -- as Mr. Emmerson put it, the sole basis is the date in those two passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's got nothing to do with the -- with the name of the Black Eagles or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. No, it's only the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In those circumstances, may it be a stipulation those two sentences, as I read into the record, appear in the transcript -- I'm sorry, appear in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke a moment ago when I said the second passage is the one I wish to take the witness to. There are two passages. I've got no objection to Mr. Emmerson's stipulation to the witness's statement about dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is that a stipulation that is supported by other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just outline to the Trial Chamber what I would propose, and that is, I accept what they're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Sometime in spring 1998 I could see there were KLA soldiers in" -- no. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The two passages are: "The first problems we had -- we had happened somewhere at the end of July or beginning of August 1998," and then: "I was at home one night at around 12.00 p.m., I think it was in late July."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those are the two passages I would -- that I wish to refer the witness to, and I have no objection to her being referred to the earlier passage about not going to school and dates and times.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the sake of clarification and absolute clarity in those circumstances, may I read three short sentences from the statement into the transcript and all parties to stipulate them. Sentence number one: "Since I did not go to school, I don't know what, for example, the months are or mean; therefore, I can't describe the time more precisely." Sentence number two: "The first problems we had happened somewhere at the end of July or beginning of August 1998 and I will now tell you about these incidents." Sentence number three: "I was at home one night around 12.00 p.m., I think it was in late July," and then the sentence continues. Those three sentences are stipulated as an admission between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please then, that's -- was the statement, and, of course, I take it that you draw the attention of the Chamber to it and you want to have them on the record because any statement about precise month where someone has said that he is not able to fully understand what the month are and limits herself to spring rather -- or early spring rather than to July, August, late July, early September, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's clear there's no question of obfuscation here. It's simply, in terms of assessing the precise reliability of dates when they have been inserted. It's important to know the background against which they're dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness put her headphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 65 ter Exhibit 1327, which is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll ask you to look at the screen, you'll see a photograph on it, I'll ask you to mark something on it with a pen. The court usher will give you a pen and I'll ask you to draw something on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, before we continue could we go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness 61, questions will now be put to you by counsel for the defendants. I do not know -- Mr. Emmerson, is it you? But before you do so, Mr. Guy-Smith, it seems that your team has been reinforced or that some strangers are in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that all who are here have been here before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I really have to apologise because this gives me a very bad reputation. Apologies. Mr. Emmerson -- Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson and I discussed the matter and he has some brief questions he would like to ask the witness and I'm more than happy to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson. You, perhaps, Witness 61, look to the left, where is Mr. Emmerson who will put some questions to you. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness 61, I've just got one or two very brief questions for you, and I'm not going to ask you any questions about your personal ordeal or what happened to you. But I just want to ask you one or two short questions about things that you have said in the past when you've spoken to investigators from the Prosecution. Now, first of all, you've been spoken to by people from the Prosecution department on more than one occasion, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're talking at the beginning, at the first time that I was interviewed. I think there were two women, two ladies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about dates and I'm not going to ask you about all of the details of who was there, but just confining yourself to the question that I ask you. You've been interviewed on more than one occasion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think if I put it to you this way, we have records of you being interviewed three times altogether, twice quite close together some years ago, and once more recently, just last year. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And each time when you were questioned, you gave answers and the answers were written down. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then at the end of the -- at the end of the process, the statement was read back to you in your own language. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then you were asked to sign the statement to say that its contents were true. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you can write your name sufficiently to sign and you did sign each one, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. On that basis, I just want to put three very, very short passages to you from what you said at the time and just get you to confirm that this is what you said. All right? First of all, when you were -- when you were interviewed in -- for the very, very first time for the record -- I'm not asking you to confirm the date, but for the record it was the 23rd of August, 2002, you said -- you described what happened to you after you left the office and after the ordeal that you have described. And what you said was this. Just listen to me for a moment. I'm going to read to you the words that you used about what happened after that. You say this, you say: "I was sent out from the office. Later I heard from my husband that he was asked basically the same questions as Toger had asked me, and I remember that he was not beaten. We were allowed to leave at around 3.00 a.m." Do you remember saying that to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The next I want to take you to is from the second statement, which was made just a little while later. Again, for the record, it was made on the 15th of October, 2002, and I'm just going to read to you what you said and signed there. This relates to your journey home after the ordeal that you've described. You said this: "When I walked home from the KLA house, I don't remember having seen anything unusual on the road." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. How can I put it? I haven't seen a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the last short passage I want to put to you comes from the statement you made most recently, just last year. And in the short passage I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, last year, I think we should not forgot that there is a 2nd of May statement as well, so therefore that could be confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- did I say the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most recently --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise. Let me make it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just bear with me a moment, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll correct what I was going to say so you're not in any way confused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson perhaps if you refer, we know the date --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to refer approximately to the seasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: About a year ago, last summer, you made a third witness statement, and for our record it's the 28th of May, 2006, and I want to ask you about a passage which appears in paragraph 5 of the statement that you signed. And you're describing your fear when you first left the house and why you say you are afraid why you might not be coming back. Okay? If you'll just bear with me more a moment. What you said was this: "I thought -- I thought that we will never come back home and that we will be killed because at that time" -- just -- just let me finish the passage first, and then I'll just ask you to confirm it. Okay. I'll start it again because I want to read it through to you in one passage. All right? I'll start again. "I thought that we will never come back home and that we will be killed because at that time a lot of people went missing and many people were killed because there was a wartime. But I cannot name any person who went missing were was killed because I almost never went out of my house. I also have never heard anything from my husband and I don't know if he was a witness of any crime." That is what your statement says. Is that what you told the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith. Now Mr. Guy-Smith, who is standing over there, will put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness 61. I'm going to be asking you a number of questions. If during the period of time that I'm asking you a question you don't understand what I've said because I've asked it perhaps poorly, please let me know because I want to make sure that you understand what I've asked you so that you can give us your best and most accurate answers. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sitting in a situation where I don't have any answer. I have a clicking -- now I have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you understand what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were -- when you went into the house, you went directly into the room - and that's a question: Did you directly go into the room where you spent some period of time speaking with this person about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Speaking with this person about whether or not you were collaborating with or having anything to do with the Serbs, as you've told us; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that room, the lights were on when you were sitting in the room; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the person that you were talking to was about a metre away from you - right? - when he was talking to you and, as you said, he was taking notes and writing down the answers to the questions he was giving you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I was on this side and he was on the other side of the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was the table about as wide as the area you're sitting in right now with -- which has the computer screen there? Was it about that wide?
