utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a little bigger. It was -- the table was bigger than this and longer than this. The -- his chair was on the other side and I was on this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, of course you are asking about the -- "was the table about as wide as the area you're sitting in," the area is approximately 2 and a half, 3 metres, but I think the witness correctly understood your question, which was not very precise, as to refer to the size of the table and the small table next to where the witness is sitting. And she finally said that it was a bit larger, and I think the measurement of approximately what we are looking at is some 1 metre 40. So the table would have been larger than 1 metre 40, 1 metre 50. May I really ask for precision --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it appears to be of such importance whether it's a metre or 2 metres, then we really should be very precise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were sitting at the table, the man who was sitting across from you was about how far away? Could you tell the Chamber how far away he was from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to put it. The table was between us like this table is in here. I was on this side and he was on the other side. I can't say how long the table was. I didn't notice it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if you use -- if you use, for example - and I'm asking you whether this works or not; if it doesn't so be it - if you were to put your arms out like this would he be that far away from you, between my two arms, or was it more than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would -- it was that big. It was not so very long and very big table. I don't know how to put it to you and how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does this look about right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was that big.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do hope somebody could estimate that; I would appreciate it because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would say it's about -- I would say it's somewhat over -- about a metre and a half is what I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A little bit over a metre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Somewhere in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A metre 70, a metre 60, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll receive the measurements of all accused counsel and witnesses at a later stage because we might need -- please proceed. It's Mr. Guy-Smith's arms spread in full. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the period of time that he was talking to you and taking notes, you could clearly see his face, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes I saw him, sometimes not, some time I was looking down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. But during that period of time when he was asking you the questions that he was asking you and notes were -- and he was taking down notes, during that period of time, if I understand it, it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of half an hour. Is that correct? Was it more? Was it less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was just in front of me sitting on the chair on the other side of the table. He was taking down notes. I don't know. He was writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the period of time that he was doing that, that he was writing and you were across the table from him, how long was that? How long were you just sitting -- the two of you just sitting in the room, with him asking you questions? How long was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe around half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith. Could you take your earphones off for a second. Mr. Guy-Smith, the Chamber gets the impression that you want to establish that the witness could have clearly seen the face and had sufficient time to see that face, and I take it that is relevant for your case because it may cast -- shed some other light on why, perhaps at a later stage, she was not -- she has not recognised that person. You spent quite a lot of time on that. The Chamber - and I've just consulted with my colleagues - have no major doubt as to under the circumstances that the witness had time and an opportunity to see who was with her in the chamber -- in that room. At the same time, memory, recollection, is -- of course you need to observe something in order to at a later stage reproduce it from memory. But you spent a lot of time on the issue which, as far as the Chamber is concerned, might not be the key issue in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if I misunderstood your line of questioning, then of course it's -- final is up to you. But I'm just telling you how the Chamber until now has perceived what you're doing and what the Chamber thinks about it as far as relevance is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If the Chamber is satisfied that, based on the evidence that has been presented, this particular witness was in the presence of that individual for some two and a half to three hours, some period of time of two and a half to three hours, when she had the ability to -- and opportunity to observe, which I think that the Chamber is understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I think if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you misunderstood. You misunderstood. First of all, the Chamber has not -- has -- at least -- I'm now speaking for myself, but I'll be corrected by my colleagues. The Chamber, on the basis of the evidence produced, might need some further thinking before it establishes that on the road at midnight that there was a full opportunity to observe a person who was among five persons, that's one. Second, if you're talking about two and a half, three hours, I think I made this estimate before, and at least from the testimony from this witness it appears that a considerable period of time was with the light switched off. So therefore, to fully observe when the light is switched off at the middle of the light and to say, Well, if the Chamber examines that the witness could have observed the person she was with for two and a half, three hours, that would be an overstatement. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as long as the light is on, and if -- as long as questions are put to you during half an hour, that the Chamber would not have great difficulties, most likely, to accept that the witness had sufficient time and was at a distance to that person to at least observe that person for half an hour. That's -- if that's what you want to establish, to be quite honest, I don't know how juries function, but it -- I think I'm speaking on behalf of the Chamber, that it does not come even to our mind that the witness would not have had an opportunity, apart from whether psychologically she was focusing on what she could have observed, whether Mr. Re has put some questions to the witness in that respect, the Chamber is not alluding in any way to how those circumstances might influence your capacity to later reproduce what you've seen. That's a different matter, but it -- I think I'm speaking on behalf of the other Judges as well that it did not come into our mind that the witness would have had no opportunity to observe the person she was with at that moment in terms of distance, in terms of light. At least during this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. The reason that I spent the time there was because, as the Chamber has correctly noted, and I was going to move to the next phase, which is with the lights off and the television on, which is what I believe the testimony was, and I was going to explore that, but the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was in the statement. I don't know whether it was in the testimony. You'll have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm -- I would like to explore that. But the reason that I -- I am doing precisely this is because of the precise, I think, underlying concerns that ultimately would come to the fore, which deals with the issue of time, memory, and the psychology of perception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm guided -- I'm guided here by consultation with an expert in the issue of eye-witness identification, who has suggested that all of these things are important for a record and important for the Chamber's determination. But I'm more than happy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's of course a difference with a jury, that this Chamber -- the members of this Chamber are not thinking for the first time in their life and not reading for the first time in their life lines on these kind of eye-witness identification, et cetera, as may be clear from earlier exchanges of view that should -- the Chamber, of course, knows the basics of theory about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you understand I'm guided -- I'm guided by Professor Wagenaar so that's the reason I'm in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. At the same time, it's time for a break. Could you please put your earphones up again. We will have a break until 1.00, and we'll then continue. Mr. Guy-Smith, is there a fair chance that we would finish today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Extremely fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we took the break, we were discussing the time when you were sitting in the room talking with this man who was asking you questions. I believe that you've -- you've told us that it was -- that there was a -- I think it was a soldier was at the door of the room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is -- the soldier who was at the door of the room, is that a soldier that you had seen earlier in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there. I saw him there, and then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was not one of the soldiers that you had seen earlier at your home before you came to the house where you were questioned, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Could you describe to the Chamber what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the door, the one at the door?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If you can, that's fine; and if you can't, that's okay too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was somewhat tall, a little stout.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of his hair? Was he -- did he have black hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about the hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say he was somewhat tall - if you could look at me for a second - do you mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- do you mean tall like me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhat a little taller than you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Taller than me? Was the man that you have said was a person who -- who put you through this ordeal, this man you said was Toger, was that -- was that man shorter than me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was short, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say he was short, he was shorter than I am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how to say now. A little -- probably -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A little shorter than I am?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, comparing the length of persons in the way you suggested could be done hardly could give any reliable results.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, given the information we have here, we work with what we have, Your Honour, and we're going to at some point approximate heights and distances and times, so I'm doing the best that I can with what we've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the other three soldiers who were at your house initially, could you describe for the Chamber what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see them. They were all the same. I didn't see them all at the same time. It was night. I didn't see them inside. I saw them only outside. Then outside it was dark. I couldn't see them so I could not tell you how they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Guy-Smith goes on, I sort of intervened a moment ago, that was when -- in relation to the height comparison evidence. All I want is for the record to reflect that when Mr. Guy-Smith was asking those questions he's standing about 15 metres away from the witness who is seated behind a screen. He is standing leaning on a lectern. I just want the record to reflect that is what he was asking the witness to comment on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. I mean, I said these kind of comparisons might not be of great assistance to the Chamber, to say the least, and then to go into further details on why not or why yes, that really doesn't assist. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had at some -- at one point earlier suggested that perhaps we take measurements of all counsel and witnesses. I think we may actually -- at some point I'm going to make a request that we do have the heights of certain people so we know what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, as far as reliability is concerned, and if we are talking about -- if we're keeping in mind that of course a period of nine or ten years might make a difference, that it's not under all circumstances, but I also leave to the parties whether they want to provide such information because it might not be totally irrelevant and the parties could also suggest that the Victims and Witnesses Section could play a role here in getting data which might -- might assist the Chamber in -- in making comparisons or assessing the reliability in respect of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you for the suggestion. I fully intended at the conclusion of today's proceedings to ask for such -- for such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, that will be in half an hour, as you are aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've told us that you were able to see some bumps on this man's face; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the bumps that you saw on this man's face, are those bumps that you were able to see on his face after the lights were turned off and the television was on in the room? Could you see the bumps then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And just so the record is clear and so that the Chamber has all the information, after the lights were turned off in the room, did the -- was the television on? Was there light coming out of the television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes it was -- yes, it was a television on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. About how far away was the television from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to say it. Maybe -- it was at the corner of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with the television on while you were in the room with this man, during that period of time, could you see his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you went through this ordeal, if I understand your testimony correctly, you left the room; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you left the room you saw your husband, I believe. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you saw your husband, did you just -- did you stay with your husband at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, but they took my husband inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after some period of time, a short period of time, and I'm asking you, you and your husband then walked home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it took you about as long to walk home as it took you to get there, about 15 or 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you got home you spoke to your father-in-law, your mother-in-law, and the other people who were about you about what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At that time did you have a chance to speak to your parents about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once, I was there only once. So my father was dead. I met only my mother and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was that still -- was that still very close to the time that this ordeal happened that you met your mother and your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very long. Maybe three or four years, maybe three or four years, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, I've just received an indication that there may be some problems with translation on page 79, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, let me just first find it. You said page 79, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm told that the answer given to my question was different than the answer that's reflected in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we -- perhaps you put the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we'll hear what her answer is. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: While Mr. Guy-Smith's looking for that, could I ask for a redaction of page 80, line 19, and page 80, lines 21 to 81, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's probably appropriate exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the most discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, then that would be a redaction page 80, line 19 up to and including 81, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Witness 61, I'm going to ask you a question that I asked you a few moments ago just to make sure that we understand completely what -- what your answer was. And the question is: And the bumps that you saw on this man's face, were those bumps that you were able to see after the lights were turned off and the television was on in the room? Could you see the bumps then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe he had them because of his shaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The information that -- the information that you gave your father-in-law and your mother-in-law about what happened to you, you never told them that when you suffered this ordeal you were a victim of many people, were you -- did you? Did you ever say anything like that to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I told them that only the Toger was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you -- do you remember after the first time that you met with investigators that the second time when you met with investigators you were shown some photos, do you remember that? That was after a few months after the first time you spoke with -- with -- I believe it was an investigator you met with. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were shown those photographs, do you remember how many photographs you were shown? You were shown about eight photographs. Does that -- is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They asked -- they asked me whether I know -- whether I know Toger. I said no. Then they showed me the photograph. I don't know how many photographs they showed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you were shown the photographs, you weren't able, after looking at the photographs, to pick out anybody in those photographs who looked like a person you called Toger, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, after the night of the ordeal, my question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to the question, I've just looked in the witness's statement; that's not what the witness's statement says. I don't object to the question, of course, but I'd simply ask Mr. Guy-Smith to put the -- what the witness says in her statement to the witness rather than: "You didn't pick out any -- anyone in those photos who looked like a person called Toger." I'm referring to the third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- I have -- I have absolutely no difficulty in doing that. I think that the question that I asked accurately reflects what happened, but for purposes of this discussion I'm happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please do it. And would you also keep in mind that -- Mr. Re, I don't know how many questions you would still have basis of what you heard in cross-examination until now but ... One here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hopefully until now there won't be too many more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were shown a sheet numbered PS1 with colour pictures of eight faces of different men, "I do not recognise any of these men." Correct? That's what you told them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith, a good photo-spread only shows people who look at least the same more or less, so if one of the accused is among them, then it would be surprising if no one looked like. Therefore, I think what Mr. Re said is correct. It was a negative result of a photo identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was a negative result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's most important, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you two or three more questions, and what I'd like you to do is I'd like you to confirm, if you could, that when you spoke to the Prosecution investigators in -- and this would be about a year ago, and I think that in terms of seasons it would have been, as Mr. Emmerson said, the summer, about a year ago, you said that: "After the night Toger raped me, I saw him often. I would see him in -- from my front yard. I would never speak to him. I usually ran back into the house. I also saw him in a car. He would often drive by the road in front of our house." That's what you told -- that's what you told the Prosecution investigators; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of a commander in the Irzniq area by the name of Shemsedin Ceku?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is he one of the people you spoke to about what happened in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, but I'm not sure. I think so. He was one of them, Shemsedin, and there were two other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to also see if you could confirm one other statement that you made to the Prosecutors, and that's paragraph 15 of the statement of May which is: "I heard that Toger was in The Hague, but I never saw a photograph of him afterwards. I've seen him on TV after Toger went to The Hague. He looks older. The person on the TV didn't look like Toger to me. He looks older. My family say that Toger was on the TV and that it is Toger in The Hague." Did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no questions. Then I -- Mr. Re, any questions on re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness 61, I just want to take you to something Mr. Emmerson asked you about, and that is when he asked you whether you had seen anything unusual on the road which -- and you said no, that was in the statement you gave earlier. What I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber, the Judges, is: How were you feeling? What was your psychological state as you were going back after what had happened to you with Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, how to say? I was not feeling well at all. I was very scared of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of things were you looking for or what were you noticing when you went -- when you went back home or what were the main thoughts in your mind when you left the KLA headquarters and were going home, on the way there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was just thinking how they could take us away. There was no need for them to take me away and for him to have his way with me in that way. This is all I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say you were not feeling well, can you give the Trial Chamber some more details about your feelings and what -- what it was that you weren't feeling -- how you weren't feeling well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know what to say. When I told my husband what had happened to me, what he had did me, of course he was feeling so sad, and my family was feeling sad as well. After that, for three years I couldn't have a child and I had to go to doctors. After I was treated by the doctors I -- I felt well after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Guy-Smith asked you a moment ago about when you were shown some photographs by some -- an investigator from the Prosecution. I just want to read to you what your statement records you as saying on the 15th of October, 2002, that's the third sentence -- third paragraph in its entirety. "When I was shown by Matti Raatikainen a sheet numbered PS1 with colour pictures of eight faces of different men, I did not recognise any of these men. I would like to point out that the rape case happened four years ago and I do feel that I would not be able to recognise anymore the perpetrator or the KLA soldiers that were with him." Now, is that what you said to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, is the -- do you think the reason you would not be able to recognise anyone could be related to the fact that it was so long --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you think four years afterwards you would have been able to recognise the person called Toger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question is, as it's presently posed, calls for, among other things, speculation on her part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I don't know to what extent. It really forwards -- forwards the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness to take her earphones off for a second. I'm just wondering the relevance of the question, Mr. Re. There are two possible answers. The first is: Yes, I think I could have been could have recognised him, then that means the negative results from the photo-spread is significant. I don't know if it's that that you were seeking to establish. Second option is she says: No, I couldn't. Then, of course, one would wonder why she thinks she couldn't. The fact is that she didn't, and further speculation on why and what could have been are perhaps more confusing than assisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it's of no assistance, I'll withdraw the question that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course if you see there is really something -- but I just pointed to you what the answers could be and also how they could be understood, and some of the questions might certainly be -- I mean, one of the answers, if you say: Yes, I could, then if you're seeking that, fine. Put the question to the witness and we'll hear the answer. If the answer is no, it's -- I don't know how to interpret or how to evaluate that. I would know how to interpret a yes, but immediately it would come into my mind how a witness who says that she could have identified someone, what's the basis for such a statement. I mean, what makes a witness say I could or I could not? Is she a psychologist? Is she -- I mean, it takes quite something to give an assessment or a judgement on what you could have done in terms of reproducing from your memory what you think you've seen once.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not pursuing it. That's the completion of my examination-in-chief -- re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Have the questions in re-examination triggered any need --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do have one request before we would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I -- let's just see whether the Bench would have any further questions. Yes, the witness has her earphones off, Mr. Emmerson, before I would engage in a line of questioning on what I have in mind, I would like to seek clarification with you because it relates to one of your questions. You have read to the witness what we find on page 61, lines 13 up till and including line 18, and the last two of these lines are: "I also have never heard anything from my husband and I don't know if he was a witness of any crime." Now, the witness has testified today what she heard from her husband. If you interpret these last two lines, you could interpret them in two ways. The first interpretation would be: My husband never told me anything about killings, disappearances, et cetera, et cetera; or you could interpret it as saying that he never told her any details. Because it follows the previous line where it reads: "But I cannot name any person who went missing or was killed because I almost never went out of my house," so she has no personal knowledge. And then you could understand the next line to be that her husband didn't gave such details to her. Now, if that's how you understand the last line, there's no need for further question; if, however, you understand this last line to mean that her husband never, ever told her anything, even without details, people being -- people missing, people killed, then I would put a few additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I understand the distinction that Your Honour is drawing. The emphasis in -- in -- or the reason for asking the question in the first place relates to the last four or five words in particular of that paragraph; in other words, I understand that to mean that her husband never told her that he was personally a witness to the commission of any crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's consistent with the testimony the witness has given today I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least there's no positive --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to suggest from this passage that he may never have referred to her instances about which he had heard hearsay accounts but without the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What we do infer from the passage is that the witness's account is that her husband never told her that he had seen or heard himself the commission of a crime as a first-hand witness. That's how I understood the passage and that's how I was intending it to be understood by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And seen or heard, you mean not heard of her --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, seen -- as in witnessing the commission of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it may be that Your Honours understand what the reason for that line of questioning is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that, but I wanted to be sure about why you read that to the witness, so see whether any further clarification is needed and it seems from --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what you tell me now, that no further clarification is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going back to the issue of measurements. I'm hoping we can get the assistance of Victims and Witnesses from the stand point of getting the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's ask the witness first whether she would --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If she would be willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you ... Witness 61, today you may have noticed that sometimes you are asked about the length of persons, et cetera, et cetera. And that's also -- in your statement, we find, and in your testimony we find elements that might be relevant. Now, the problem is that we do not know exactly what your length, at least, at this moment is. Would you mind that once you've left this courtroom that, with the assistance of the Victims and Witnesses Section, that they would just measure what your height is so that at least the Chamber would know and is in a position to better assess and evaluate your testimony. Would you mind if someone would just measure you, write it down, and give it to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I have to address the parties. What would be the appropriate way of introducing this information to the Chamber? Mr. Guy-Smith, would it be necessary to call one of the persons of the Victims and Witnesses Section to testify about it; or would a brief written report --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe a brief written report is a stipulation between parties would suffice. I have full confidence that they will be in a position to make an accurate measurement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, similar position, I do understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course in order to compare -- and, of course, that's another matter, Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to make myself available to the same section so that they can measure me, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, it's not only you but, I mean, length of persons gains some relevance in respect of one of the accused as well. That, of course, is a matter -- I don't know whether it's somewhere on the record. I don't know whether you are intending to provide that information to the Chamber. I think it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- should be in your hand. Okay. Then we leave that initiative to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please inform the Victims and Witnesses Section that the Chamber would highly appreciate if we would know what the exact length of this witness is and that she -- that she gave her consent for measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I would like to thank the witness because I'm also looking at the clock. Witness 61, you've come to The Hague to testify. I'd like to thank you very much for having done so and very having answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to have answered the questions of both parties and the questions -- well, only a few questions of the Bench. Therefore, thank you and I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Guy-Smith, for the witness to leave, we would have to pull the curtains down. Is there anything at this moment, because otherwise we could just adjourn and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. The last issue only dealt with one of the -- is really a thank you to one of my interns whose last day it was today, since she's somebody who rarely gets to come to court and that's Mia Ter Haar and I just wanted to indicate my thanks to her on the record because she's worked very hard on this case and we're going to hate to see her to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith, I gave it some thought today, what it means if you don't remember faces. If there's no other procedural matter to be discussed, Madam Registrar, we will adjourn until Monday, the 14th of May, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of May, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
